summary: Sleeping-car magnate George Pullman built a controlling company town near Chicago, then cut wages without cutting rents in 1893-94, sparking a national railway strike crushed by federal troops.

evidence.note: Pullman's birth in 1831 in upstate New York opens the biography
1880 land purchase and construction of the company town begins the core story
segment on Black porters paid a fraction of white conductors' wages
town restricted to white residents; later the union votes to exclude Black workers
long reading of an 1880s Atlantic column on the labor question; later press framing of the strike
28 percent wage cut with rents unchanged, workers pushed into debt to the company
extended segment on Debs' background and founding of the American Railway Union
1894 commission, 1898 court ruling on the town and Pullman's 1897 death and burial close the story

notes: Title names the strike but the episode is built as a Pullman biography, so both are primary. Transcript says the town was incorporated into Chicago in 1898 by the Illinois Supreme Court; historically annexation was 1889 and the 1898 ruling forced the company to sell the town. Covered span ends 1898 per the transcript. Federal troops and the injunction have no clean theme fit.
